claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by early reduction of Pt, Ir, or Ru precursors.
Early-reduced Pt, Ir, or Ru forms an initial metallic lattice capable of activating hydrogen.
Hydrogen spillover from the initial noble-metal lattice reduces adjacent Ni, Co, Cu, and Fe ions.
The reduced less-noble metals incorporate into the preformed lattice to produce a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Pd has poor or unfavorable hydrogen-desorption kinetics relative to Pt, Ir, or Ru.
Replacing the effective noble-metal precursor with Pd disrupts spillover-mediated reduction and causes phase separation.
Spray drying the mixed salts produces nearly spherical and compositionally uniform precursor particles.
The stated spray-drying and hydrogen-reduction route forms a porous, self-supported three-dimensional nanoframework composed of nanoarms.
The nanoarms exhibit homogeneous elemental distributions.
Pt- and Ir-based alloys formed by this route have an FCC lattice, whereas Ru-based alloys have an HCP lattice.
Pt-, Ir-, or Ru-seeded formulations will form homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles under the specified reduction conditions.
The Pt-, Ir-, or Ru-seeded products will have a well-integrated porous nanostructure.
The Pt-, Ir-, or Ru-seeded products will exhibit greater methanol-oxidation mass activity than commercial Pt black and the analogous Pd-substituted products.
The Pd-substituted formulation will produce phase-separated or multiphase material with uncontrolled morphology.
The cited commercial Pt black benchmark has a methanol-oxidation mass activity of 170 mA/mgPt.
Prior noble-metal-free or Pd-containing control systems have been shown to yield phase-separated materials.
The proposed mechanism applies to spray-dried, hydrogen-reduced noble metal–based systems seeded with Pt, Ir, or Ru and containing as many as eight elements.
The FCC-to-HCP transformation has an estimated energy barrier of approximately 0.45 eV.
